e.etymology: A short form of Genevieve or of its Spanish form Genoveva.
From Old Norse dagr, day, and maer, maid. Queen Dagmar of Denmark, a Bohemian princess who took the name on her marriage in 1205, made it popular.
A spelling of Denise, the French feminine of Denis, from the Greek name Dionysios, a follower of Dionysus, god of wine.
A feminine form of Herman, from the Germanic words hari, army, and man, man.
A blend of girl and midget, the surf-crowd nickname of Kathy Kohner. Her father's 1957 novel Gidget, the films and the 1965 Sally Field TV series spread it as a given name.

assoc.t: Gidget, the surfer girl of 1950s-60s novels, films and TV

e.note: The name is built on midget, a word now considered offensive.

e.etymology: The English form of Welsh Merfyn, the name of a 9th-century king of Gwynedd. Its original meaning is uncertain.
A spelling of Latoya, an American name built from the prefix La- and Toya. The singer La Toya Jackson made it widely known around 1980.
A spelling of Larry, the pet form of Lawrence, from the Roman name Laurentius, a man from Laurentum, an ancient town near Rome.
A spelling of Dorothy that follows the two-syllable pronunciation. Dorothy is the English form of Greek Dorothea, from doron, gift, and theos, god.
A spelling of Cheryl, a 20th-century English name that probably blends Cherie or Cherry with the ending of Beryl.
A spelling of Sherry, an English respelling of French cherie, darling, that was also taken to be the name of the Spanish wine.
The short form of Geoffrey, the older British spelling of Jeffrey. The Normans brought the name to England; it ends in the Germanic word for peace, and its first part is uncertain.
e.note: Americans who have not met the spelling sometimes read it as GEE-off.

e.etymology: A pet form of Florence, from Latin florens, flourishing, and of Flora, from flos, flower.
A pet form of Darrell or Darren.
namesakes: Darry Curtis (the oldest brother in S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders)
e.note: Pronounced the same as the word dairy.

e.etymology: The German and French feminine of Herman, from the Germanic words hari, army, and man, man.
Not a true given name. It comes from birth records in which an unnamed newborn boy was entered as Male and the placeholder was never replaced with a name.
e.note: A records placeholder for an unnamed baby boy, and the ordinary English word male.

e.etymology: A spelling of Irene, from Greek eirene, peace, the name of the Greek goddess of peace and of several early saints.
A spelling of Johnny, the pet form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A spelling of Margie, the pet form of Margaret and Marjorie, from Greek margarites, pearl.
Spanish for little lady, from dama. In the United States it followed the singer Damita Jo, who had hits in 1960 and 1961; Janet Jackson's middle names are Damita Jo.
A spelling of Buddy, the American word for a friend, probably a child's form of brother, long used as a boy's nickname and then as a given name.
The French form of Ferdinand, a name the Visigoths carried to Spain, from Germanic words for journey and for daring.
A surname used as a first name. The English surname is a form of Mayhew, from Matthew; County Mayo in Ireland takes its name from Irish Maigh Eo, plain of the yew trees.

assoc.t: mayo, the everyday short word for mayonnaise
Mayo Clinic, the Minnesota medical center

e.note: Mayo is the everyday word for mayonnaise, so jokes are likely.

e.etymology: A spelling of Aline, a medieval short form of Adeline, which rests on the Germanic word adal, noble.
A form of German Elfriede, which comes from the Old English name Aelfthryth, made of aelf, elf, and thryth, strength.
An American name that blends Shawn with the sound of Chante, French for sung.
An American coinage of the 1980s that puts the prefix Sha- before Tara.
